articles.title: French Expression of the Day: Être à la bourre
articles.text:
French Expression of the Day: Être à la bourre
Advertisement
French Word of the Day
Members only
French Expression of the Day: Être à la bourre
The Local France - news@thelocal.fr
Published: 13 Nov, 2026 CET.
Updated: Sat 14 Nov 2026 06:26 CET
Add a comment
Photo: Annie Spratt/Unsplash/ Nicolas Raymond
Add The Local as a preferred source
If you’re somebody who has a small (or big) problem with punctuality, then this French expression is for you.
Why do I need to know être à la bourre?
If you don’t have time for a conversation but don’t want to be rude, or need to tell your cabbie to step on it, letting somebody know that you are à la bourre will quickly explain your predicament.
What does it mean?
Être à la bourre – roughly pronounced eh-truh ah la boh-rruh (listen here) – translates exactly as "to be in the stuffing," which might sound a bit nonsensical.
Advertisement
To be à la bourre has little to do with with this basic meaning; it’s actually a colloquial way to say that you’re 'running late' or 'in a hurry', the two usually being related. It is typically used with the verb être (‘to be’).
The roots of this expression are a bit murky, but most experts believe that être à la bourre comes from a card game popular in the southwestern French region of Occitanie (around Toulouse and Montpellier), called "la borra" in the local Occitan language.
According to one theory, the player who was behind (and therefore losing money) was "a la borra," and this is how the expression made its way into everyday French.
Another has it that when someone was running late, the people waiting for them assumed that they had gotten caught up playing cards somewhere. Either way, être à la bourre eventually spread throughout the rest of France, and is heard all over the country today.
Before using this expression, you should keep in mind that être à la bourre, while not vulgar, is certainly familiar, so it’s probably more appropriate for a conversation with your co-worker than with your boss.
Don't miss our journalists' daily news roundup from France
If you need to say that you’re running late more formally, you can explain that you’re en retard (‘late’) or that you’re pressé (‘in a hurry’).
Use it like this
Excuse-moi, il faut que je m'en aille, je suis vachement à la bourre. – Sorry, I have to go, I’m really running late.
Si on ne part pas maintenant, on va être à la bourre au travail. – If we don’t leave now, we’re going to be late to work.
Essoufflé et tout rouge, il avait l’air d’être à la bourre. – Out of breath and flushed, he looked like he was in a hurry.
Je suis désolé d’être à la bourre, il y avait un bouchon affreux sur le périphérique. – Sorry for being late, there was an awful traffic jam on the ring road.

articles.title: Why Berlin is still a magnet for international talent
articles.text:
Why Berlin is still a magnet for international talent
Presented by Talent Berlin
Why Berlin is still a magnet for international talent
There's far more to Berlin than its UNESCO-protected club culture. For those seeking an exciting career move, the German capital offers a heady mix of both business and pleasure.
Published: Thu 29 Oct 2026 15:45 CEST
Photo: Talent Berlin
For some, living and working abroad is a lifelong dream. It’s choosing where to start this new life that’s the million-dollar question. A city might offer great job opportunities but fall short on other things that make life outside work fulfilling—or vice versa.
In Berlin, you don't have to choose. As one of Europe's capitals for innovation and start-ups, it combines career opportunities with a rich cultural scene, more to do outside of work than one could manage in a lifetime, and a diverse international community ( around 25 per cent of Berliners are foreign-born).
It’s a city that’s famous for its tolerance and readiness to embrace different lifestyles. After all, Berliners aren't born—they're made at the Bürgeramt.
A city buzzing with ideas
Berlin's reputation as a start-up capital isn't just hype. In 2026, StartupBlink named it the EU's "Best Community-Driven Ecosystem". Its venture-backed start-ups are worth €169 billion and support some 94,000 jobs.
The Talent Berlin LinkedIn page posts Jobs of the Week, as well as other useful information about what's happening in Berlin's talent and innovation ecosystem.
Explore the Berlin-Brandenburg start-up ecosystem
While Berlin is home to one of Europe's leading start-up hubs, its business landscape is as varied as it is prolific. It has a booming tech sector, world-class life sciences and biotech communities, a growing green economy, and, famously, a thriving creative scene.
The city practically pulses with ideas and innovation; it's an incredibly exciting place to be for those working in science and research, biotechnology, and energy and environment, as well as other industries that will play a vital role in the decades to come.
Many of Berlin's innovations emerge where these industries intersect, from sustainable fashion and food science to digital health and the creative use of AI.
International professionals working in the city often cite its cross-sector ecosystem as one of its greatest advantages. Once you have your foot in the door, you can hop between start-ups, established companies, research, and emerging industries.
Photo: Talent Berlin
You won't get lost in translation
Learning a new language is all part of the fun of moving abroad, and German is, naturally, widely spoken in Berlin.
However, in those early days — or even years — of acclimatisation, you can easily get by in English, though it doesn't hurt to have a German-speaking friend who can help with certain administrative tasks.
Taking the time to learn German doesn't just expand your career options and make bureaucracy easier; it helps you integrate into Germany itself, not just Berlin's international community.
Keep up with Berlin’s start-up scene
If you’re serious about settling in Berlin for the long term, an integration or language course gives you essential German skills and practical knowledge of German society to help you live and work independently.
The city that never sleeps
In Berlin, when the 9-to-5 ends, the 5-to-9 begins.
Whatever you like to do in your spare time, whether you're into climbing, clubbing, or quite literally anything in between, you'll find it in Berlin.
The city’s tree-lined streets are crammed with cafes, bars, restaurants, and indie stores. Parks punctuate the city, and you're rarely more than a short journey from a wild swimming lake, forest, or nature reserve where you can enjoy the great outdoors.
Photo: Paula Schmidt / Pexels
Many Berliners forgo a car for a bike; the city is easy to cycle, and an extensive, affordable public transport system makes getting around without a car relatively straightforward.
The elephant in the room
Berlin is an attractive place to live, so its housing market is stretched—to put it lightly. That makes it tough to find somewhere to live, especially for newcomers.
Somewhat counterintuitively, you generally need to be in Berlin while searching for an apartment, so you can view the property and meet the landlord or estate agent before signing.
Many people start with temporary accommodation while they familiarise themselves with the rental process and look for a long-term contract.
Check with your employer about any relocation or housing assistance they may offer, and take a look at Talent Berlin's housing guide as a starting point. The organisation also offers a housing service your employer may already use, so it’s worth asking about this before you make the move.
Could Berlin be your next move?
Berlin has its quirks — some that make life easier, others that can make it more challenging. But for skilled professionals, few cities offer the same combination of career opportunity, innovation, internationalism, and life beyond work.
You may move to Berlin for the job, but it won't be the only reason you stay.

articles.title: Inside France: Why French voters are holding out for a hero
articles.text:
Inside France: Why French voters are holding out for a hero
Advertisement
Inside France
Members only
Inside France: Why French voters are holding out for a hero
Emma Pearson - emma.pearson@thelocal.com
Published: 14 Nov, 2026 CET.
Add a comment
The memorial of French resistance leader Jean Moulin at the Eure-et-Loire prefecture in Chartres, central France, where he was the Préfet before the war. Photo by JEAN-FRANCOIS MONIER / AFP
Add The Local as a preferred source
From the search for a saviour within the tangled mess of French politics to the return to icons from history, via a French cultural milestone, here is our weekly look at the news and talking points from France.
Inside France is editor Emma Pearson's weekly look at some of the news, talking points and gossip in France that you might not have heard about. It’s published each Saturday and members can receive it directly to their inbox, by going to their newsletter preferences or adding their email to the sign-up box in this article.
I don't think I'm the only person in France who this week learned that the outfit one wears for judo is called judogi (and not, apparently, pyjamas).
The reason for this sudden interest in martial arts is, of course, the surprise presidential bid of French judo star Teddy Riner - already a massively popular figure as well as a stunningly successful sportsman, Riner's early polling tops 20 percent, putting him second in the polls behind only Marine Le Pen.
Don't miss our journalists' daily news roundup from France
Before we get too excited, he hasn't actually announced any detailed policies beyond his 'ni de gauche, ni de droite' (neither left nor right) launch speech. And there is plenty of time for scandals to emerge or him to make gaffes and generally get caught out.
That initial polling success speaks, I think, to a general sense of the French electorate being sick of all politicians, and explains at least in part why 'les extrèmes' of the far-right and the far-left are leading the polls - neither of them has yet had a go at running France, and therefore neither of them has messed it up.
That's despite both of them touting economic policies that have variously been described as 'fantasy land' or economic suicide.
READ ALSO: OPINION: France's failing centre is to blame for popularity of Mélenchon's fantasy economics
It feels that there is increasing hunger for a 'saviour' from outside the system to come and somehow sort out the tangled mess of French politics, which might explain the interest in Christine Lagarde stepping down early from her job as head of the European Central Bank. She's being widely discussed as a possible candidate, despite not having made any announcement and despite the timeline making it extremely difficult for her to stand.
Advertisement
Talking France
We discuss the economic programme of Jean-Luc Mélenchon and La France Insoumise in this week's Talking France podcast, as well as the latest from the protests and the new-look TGV train. Listen here.
We also discuss all the French World War Two films in cinemas right now, and what it says about the current political climate. Since we recorded, I have seen Moulin - about the French Resistance leader Jean Moulin and his capture and torture at the hands of the Nazi commander Klaus Barbie - and I don't think it was the best of the bunch.
In my opinion, criticism of its "gratuitous violence" is a little unfair. It was telling the story of real life events that were very brutal (the film's torture scenes are mild compared to what they actually did to Jean Moulin) but it's something of a hagiography. That might be historically accurate but makes the film a little flat.
A shame, because the real Jean Moulin's life was incredible, and he deserves a better film.
My pick of the bunch remains Notre Salut - a complicated, unsettling and unusual film about a Vichy collaborator.
A milestone très français
I also achieved a French cultural milestone this week - a trip to France's national theatre the Comédie française to see a Molière play. I was a little worried about whether I'd understand it all, and had deliberately picked a lighter comedy, Les Fourberies de Scapin, which turned out to be very accessible and funny (people fell over, had buckets put on their heads and a man was put in a bag and beaten with sticks - this is absolutely my level of comedy).
Advertisement
The interior of the building is truly beautiful, and open for tours for those who feel that their French isn't yet up to a play. And for those outside Paris, you can catch a glimpse of the workings of this historic theatre in the recent comedy film De la comédie française.
Thanks for reading, and bon weekend

Talking France is a free podcast produced by The Local

The Talking France podcast is back, exploring what France might look like under a far-left president, the latest developments on strikes and protests, and what the recent wave of WWII films tells us about the country's current political climate.
Host Ben McPartland is joined by The Local France's Emma Pearson, Emma Albright, and politics expert John Lichfield to discuss the latest from France.
You can find the Talking France podcast on Spotify, Apple or the French platform  Deezer or on  World Radio Paris. You can download it here or listen to the full episode on the link below.
We start by discussing the latest potential candidate to enter France's 2027 presidential race: five-time Olympic judo champion Teddy Riner. Why is he running? Why is he so popular with the French public? And, perhaps most importantly, does he even have a chance at becoming president?
Stay informed with our essential Talking France newsletter
Sticking with politics, this week far-left party La France Insoumise (LFI) published its full manifesto in book form. We break down some of its key policies and what they could mean for foreigners living in France. We also look at its economic proposals, environmental ambitions and social policies.
More strikes and protests have been announced for November. We bring you the latest developments, as well as the government's announcements aimed at easing tensions and addressing public anger.
You may have noticed that several French films about the Second World War have recently arrived in cinemas. Is this simply a coincidence, or does it have something to do with France's current political climate? We take a closer look at the films and report on what two experts say about the wider significance of these releases.
Advertisement
Finally, we turn to trains, with a look at the unveiling and launch of France's new high-speed TGV-M. The next generation of TGV promises a range of new features and improvements. We take a closer look at what's new.

articles.title: OPINION: France's failing centre is to blame for popularity of Mélenchon's fantasy economics
articles.text:
OPINION: France's failing centre is to blame for popularity of Mélenchon's fantasy economics
Advertisement
Politics
Members only
OPINION: France's failing centre is to blame for popularity of Mélenchon's fantasy economics
John Lichfield - news@thelocal.fr
Published: 12 Nov, 2026 CET.
Updated: Thu 12 Nov 2026 09:01 CET
4 comments
Leftist party La France Insoumise (LFI) candidate in France's 2027 presidential election Jean-Luc Melenchon presenting his manifesti in Le Bourget, in the outskirts of Paris on November 7, 2026. Photo by Kenzo TRIBOUILLARD / AFP
Add The Local as a preferred source
The manifesto from the far left candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon has been slammed as 'economic suicide' for France - so why is he so popular, asks John Lichfield.
According to the opinion polls France will face a choice next May between two forms of national suicide: Mélenchon v Le Pen.
We were presented last month with Marine Le Pen’s dishonest arithmetic and incoherent jumble of liberalism and protectionism, tax cuts and increased social spending.
Last week, Jean-Luc Mélenchon published a six-year-old’s Santa Claus wish-list as the ultra-left economic programme of his “New France”.
READ ALSO: Nuclear, minimum wage and citizenship: Jean-Luc Mélenchon's 2027 manifesto
A country which already works less than its neighbours would move to retirement at 60; to a 32-hour week; a sixth week’s holiday; and seven days’ compassionate leave for the death of a “friend”.
A country which already entrusts 57 percent of its GDP to the state would add at least €100 billion a year to its annual budget. Prices would be frozen. Salaries increased. A large chunk of the national debt would be repudiated.
Who would pay? Private enterprise and “the rich” - several times over it seems. Tax breaks for business would be abolished. Inheritance would be limited to €12 million. There would be at least two new taxes on “wealth” plus higher income tax for moderate to high earners. Some industries, including banks, would be nationalised.
Advertisement
To give Mélenchon credit, his programme is coherent in a way. It is an unashamed lurch towards the kind of “collectivism” (his own word) last attempted in Europe by the Soviet Union.
By contrast, Le Pen’s programme is a straightforward swindle – a bait and switch mixture of welfarism and liberalism, explained in numbers which don’t add up. More on that next week.
The La France Insoumise (LFI) economic plan is ideologically coherent but self-defeating. It makes sweeping promises to young people, including university places for all and a minimum income for the over-18s. It guarantees them a miserable future by transferring an even greater share of national resources to the inactive old.
The Mélenchon economic plan cuts the ground from under its own feet in other ways. It promises a rapid dash to 100 percent renewable energy AND the dismantlement of France’s nuclear power stations (which are responsible for 70 percent of the nation’s electricity). It expects other EU countries to agree to abolish part of French debt while France unilaterally repudiates the single European market for goods and capital.
In sum, rule by the LFI would rapidly mean rule by the IMF. “Mélenchonomics” is simultaneously less dangerous than “Marinomics” and more dangerous.
Don't miss John Lichfield's expert French politics analysis
It is less dangerous because Mélenchon will never be elected and the programme will never be implemented. If he does reach the second round, the polls suggest that he will be defeated by Le Pen by a two to one margin.
It is more dangerous because it is NOT intended as a programme for democratic government. Mélenchon knows that he cannot be elected this May; he wants only to reach the second round.
By exciting the idealistic Left and especially the young, he believes that he can overwhelm the muddled promises of central bloc candidates, handicapped by their at least partial attachment to the real world.
Once in Round Two, the LFI will paint anyone who abstains or votes Le Pen as a “neo-liberal” or a “fascist” and a “racist”. Mélenchon knows that he will still lose. He expects to emerge post-election as the only credible voice of “opposition to fascism” and to foment an insurrectionary mood which will make the street protests of recent weeks appear feeble.
An obvious question arises. If Le Pen and Mélenchon are offering such dotty programmes for government, why are they attracting the support of well over 50 percent of the French electorate? According to the most recent opinion polls, Le Pen has 35 percent support in the first round of the presidential election on April 18th. Mélenchon had risen in the last month from circa 14 percent to 19 percent, fuelled by his 45 percent support amongst under-24s and by the protests against failing lycées and the cost of living.
Advertisement
No candidate in a crowded but flailing “mainstream” – from the centre-left to centre-right via the ex-Macronist centre – is currently attracting more than 14 percent of the Round One vote.
As things stand, France is heading for a calamitous choice in the two-candidate second round on May 2nd between two ways of pretending that elephants can fly. Why?
All three forms of the mainstream, centre-right, centre-left and centre, have governed the country this century. They are held co-responsible for the €3.6 trillion mountain of debt. They have jointly fashioned a bizarre situation where the French state claims more resources than almost any other European country but still struggles to meet national needs in education, health and defence.
France is NOT the basket-case that some claim. In terms of the UN’s Human Development Index of economic and social success it comes in the top quarter, at 26th, close to other large western nations. Poverty is growing but remains below the EU average. The country still has a powerful industrial base, from defence, to luxury goods, to cars, to aircraft.

The manifesto from the far left candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon has been slammed as 'economic suicide' for France - so why is he so popular, asks John Lichfield.
According to the opinion polls France will face a choice next May between two forms of national suicide: Mélenchon v Le Pen.
We were presented last month with Marine Le Pen’s dishonest arithmetic and incoherent jumble of liberalism and protectionism, tax cuts and increased social spending.
Last week, Jean-Luc Mélenchon published a six-year-old’s Santa Claus wish-list as the ultra-left economic programme of his “New France”.
READ ALSO: Nuclear, minimum wage and citizenship: Jean-Luc Mélenchon's 2027 manifesto
A country which already works less than its neighbours would move to retirement at 60; to a 32-hour week; a sixth week’s holiday; and seven days’ compassionate leave for the death of a “friend”.
A country which already entrusts 57 percent of its GDP to the state would add at least €100 billion a year to its annual budget. Prices would be frozen. Salaries increased. A large chunk of the national debt would be repudiated.
Who would pay? Private enterprise and “the rich” - several times over it seems. Tax breaks for business would be abolished. Inheritance would be limited to €12 million. There would be at least two new taxes on “wealth” plus higher income tax for moderate to high earners. Some industries, including banks, would be nationalised.
Advertisement
To give Mélenchon credit, his programme is coherent in a way. It is an unashamed lurch towards the kind of “collectivism” (his own word) last attempted in Europe by the Soviet Union.
By contrast, Le Pen’s programme is a straightforward swindle – a bait and switch mixture of welfarism and liberalism, explained in numbers which don’t add up. More on that next week.
The La France Insoumise (LFI) economic plan is ideologically coherent but self-defeating. It makes sweeping promises to young people, including university places for all and a minimum income for the over-18s. It guarantees them a miserable future by transferring an even greater share of national resources to the inactive old.
The Mélenchon economic plan cuts the ground from under its own feet in other ways. It promises a rapid dash to 100 percent renewable energy AND the dismantlement of France’s nuclear power stations (which are responsible for 70 percent of the nation’s electricity). It expects other EU countries to agree to abolish part of French debt while France unilaterally repudiates the single European market for goods and capital.
In sum, rule by the LFI would rapidly mean rule by the IMF. “Mélenchonomics” is simultaneously less dangerous than “Marinomics” and more dangerous.
Don't miss John Lichfield's expert French politics analysis
It is less dangerous because Mélenchon will never be elected and the programme will never be implemented. If he does reach the second round, the polls suggest that he will be defeated by Le Pen by a two to one margin.
It is more dangerous because it is NOT intended as a programme for democratic government. Mélenchon knows that he cannot be elected this May; he wants only to reach the second round.
By exciting the idealistic Left and especially the young, he believes that he can overwhelm the muddled promises of central bloc candidates, handicapped by their at least partial attachment to the real world.
Once in Round Two, the LFI will paint anyone who abstains or votes Le Pen as a “neo-liberal” or a “fascist” and a “racist”. Mélenchon knows that he will still lose. He expects to emerge post-election as the only credible voice of “opposition to fascism” and to foment an insurrectionary mood which will make the street protests of recent weeks appear feeble.
An obvious question arises. If Le Pen and Mélenchon are offering such dotty programmes for government, why are they attracting the support of well over 50 percent of the French electorate? According to the most recent opinion polls, Le Pen has 35 percent support in the first round of the presidential election on April 18th. Mélenchon had risen in the last month from circa 14 percent to 19 percent, fuelled by his 45 percent support amongst under-24s and by the protests against failing lycées and the cost of living.
Advertisement
No candidate in a crowded but flailing “mainstream” – from the centre-left to centre-right via the ex-Macronist centre – is currently attracting more than 14 percent of the Round One vote.
As things stand, France is heading for a calamitous choice in the two-candidate second round on May 2nd between two ways of pretending that elephants can fly. Why?
All three forms of the mainstream, centre-right, centre-left and centre, have governed the country this century. They are held co-responsible for the €3.6 trillion mountain of debt. They have jointly fashioned a bizarre situation where the French state claims more resources than almost any other European country but still struggles to meet national needs in education, health and defence.
France is NOT the basket-case that some claim. In terms of the UN’s Human Development Index of economic and social success it comes in the top quarter, at 26th, close to other large western nations. Poverty is growing but remains below the EU average. The country still has a powerful industrial base, from defence, to luxury goods, to cars, to aircraft.

Two British businessmen have been formally charged over a suspected fraud of €16 million centred on a château in south-west France.
Back in May, after a lengthy investigation into potential fraud and money laundering, a British businessman was arrested in Spain and extradited back to France.
Now, the man and his business partner have been charged (mis en examen) in France in relation to the case, after a court hearing in Bordeaux in early November.
Former police officer Robin Barrasford, 56, was charged with 'fraud and money laundering by an organised group'. He has been released on bail of €250,000 and has been banned from leaving French territory.
Advertisement
His business partner Alan Bird, 79, was also charged and released on a bail bond of €800,000 - his bail conditions state that he can only leave France for trips to the UK and back.
Both deny the charges. Their lawyer Julien Plouton told the court that they intend to argue that the scheme was a good faith business enterprise that ended in “a commercial collapse linked to the economic climate”.
The alleged fraud centres on a château in Noth, near Limoges in south-west France, which the two Brits bought for €2.5 million.
They created brochures showing a planned luxury golf and spa retreat - the Halcyon Retreat and Golf Spa - complete with private chalets in the woods surrounding the château, and began advertising for investors, promising them free use of the chalets as well as a hefty profit on their investments in the luxury development.
Stay ahead of the news on buying & owning property in France
But according to the financial crimes unit in Limoges, work never even began on the site and instead the cash from investors - estimated to be around €16 million - was funnelled into a network of offshore bank accounts.
The Local has spoken to several people who invested their life savings in the project, hoping for a retirement home or a property investment, and were left with nothing.
